claims.statement: Opt-in full-RBF allows a spender to replace an unconfirmed transaction by spending the same inputs under a specific policy.

evidence.quote:
Many nodes today will not replace any transaction in their mempool with
another transaction that spends the same inputs, making it difficult for
spenders to adjust their previously-sent transactions to deal with
unexpected confirmation delays or to perform other useful replacements.

The opt-in full Replace-by-Fee (opt-in full-RBF) signaling policy
described here allows spenders to add a signal to a transaction indicating
that they want to be able to replace that transaction in the future.

claims.statement: BIP 125 is mempool policy rather than consensus; nodes may choose whether to allow replacements.

evidence.quote: Nodes may allow transactions containing this signal to be replaced in their mempools.

claims.statement: A transaction explicitly signals replaceability when any input has nSequence below 0xfffffffe.

evidence.quote: A transaction is considered to have opted in to allowing replacement of itself if any of its inputs have an nSequence number less than (0xffffffff - 1).

claims.statement: A transaction can inherit replaceability from an ancestor only while that ancestor remains unconfirmed.

evidence.quote: Transactions that don't explicitly signal replaceability are replaceable under this policy for as long as any one of their ancestors signals replaceability and remains unconfirmed.

claims.statement: Inherited replaceability ends only when no opt-in ancestor remains unconfirmed; confirming one ancestor does not erase another unconfirmed ancestor’s signal.

evidence.quote: as long as any one of their ancestors signals replaceability and remains unconfirmed

claims.statement: The teaching model validates ancestry references and rejects cycles before evaluating replacement gates.

evidence.quote: as long as any one of their ancestors signals replaceability and remains unconfirmed

claims.statement: Wallets that do not want replaceability should use 0xffffffff or the locktime-compatible 0xfffffffe and avoid other people’s unconfirmed replaceable inputs.

evidence.quote:
Wallets that don't want to signal replaceability should use either a max sequence number (0xffffffff) or a sequence number of (0xffffffff-1) when they also want to use locktime; all known wallets currently do this.
They should also take care not to spend any unconfirmed transaction that signals replaceability explicitly or through inherited signaling; most wallets also currently do this by not spending any unconfirmed transactions except for those they created themselves.

claims.statement: A replacement may include an unconfirmed input only if that input was included in one of the original transactions.

evidence.quote: The replacement transaction may only include an unconfirmed input if that input was included in one of the original transactions.

claims.statement: A replacement must pay an absolute fee of at least the sum paid by the original transactions.

evidence.quote: The replacement transaction pays an absolute fee of at least the sum paid by the original transactions.

claims.statement: A replacement must pay for its own bandwidth at the node’s minimum relay fee rate in addition to the original fees.

evidence.quote: The replacement transaction must also pay for its own bandwidth at or above the rate set by the node's minimum relay fee setting.

claims.statement: At 1 satoshi/byte and 500 bytes, a replacement must pay at least 500 satoshis more than the originals.

evidence.quote: For example, if the minimum relay fee is 1 satoshi/byte and the replacement transaction is 500 bytes total, then the replacement must pay a fee at least 500 satoshis higher than the sum of the originals.

claims.statement: A higher fee rate does not excuse failing the absolute bandwidth-bump requirement.

evidence.quote:
The replacement transaction pays an absolute fee of at least the sum paid by the original transactions.
# The replacement transaction must also pay for its own bandwidth at or above the rate set by the node's minimum relay fee setting.

claims.statement: The number of originals and descendants evicted by a replacement must not exceed 100 transactions.

evidence.quote: The number of original transactions to be replaced and their descendant transactions which will be evicted from the mempool must not exceed a total of 100 transactions.

claims.statement: Receiving wallets should treat opt-in full-RBF payments with additional suspicion or ignore them until confirmed.

evidence.quote:
Wallets that display unconfirmed transactions to users or that provide data about unconfirmed transactions to automated systems should consider doing one of the following:

# Conveying additional suspicion about opt-in full-RBF transactions to the user or data consumer.

# Ignoring the opt-in transaction until it has been confirmed.

claims.statement: Signaling and passing the policy do not guarantee replacement propagation or confirmation.

evidence.quote:
Actual replacement may be unreliable until two conditions have been satisfied:

# Enough nodes have upgraded to support it, providing a relay path for replacements to go from spending wallets to miners controlling significant amounts of hash rate.

# Enough hash rate has upgraded to support replacement, allowing for reasonable probability that a replacement can be mined.

claims.statement: BIP 125’s nSequence signaling is compatible with consensus-enforced locktimes but is a separate mechanism from them.

evidence.quote: There are no known problematic interactions between opt-in full-RBF and other uses of nSequence. Specifically, opt-in full-RBF is compatible with consensus-enforced locktime as provided in the Bitcoin 0.1 implementation, BIP68 (Relative lock-time using consensus-enforced sequence numbers), and BIP112 (CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY).
